planting.note: Set divisions in part shade once soil has warmed; give the pale variegated leaves some relief from hot afternoon sun to avoid scorch.

directions: One of the older ajuga selections still in circulation, 'Variegata' carries soft gray-green leaves broadly mottled with cream, a quieter pattern than the bronze or purple-toned tricolor ajugas now more common in the trade. Short spikes of blue to violet flowers rise just above the foliage mat in late spring. Growth is slower and less aggressive than the straight species, so it rarely becomes weedy in a bed. Divide congested clumps every few years to keep the variegation bright and prevent the center from thinning out.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in part shade in spring; the thick, textured leaves hold up well under tree canopies once established.

directions: This selection is grown mainly for its thick, deeply quilted purple leaves, which have a heavier, more puckered texture than the smoother foliage of most garden ajugas. Short spikes of the typical blue bugleweed flowers appear in late spring above the foliage mat. The dense, textured leaves make a strong textural contrast when paired with fine-leaved ferns or grassy groundcovers nearby. Like other ajugas, it spreads by surface runners and benefits from occasional thinning to keep the planting from becoming overly thick.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set divisions in part shade in spring; foliage bronzing is most pronounced where the planting gets a bit of morning sun.

directions: This older cultivar stands apart from most garden ajugas by its rose-red to pink flower spikes, a warmer color than the blue or violet blooms typical of the species. Leaves are dark green tinged with bronze, deepening further in cooler weather. It forms a dense, low mat by surface runners and knits together quickly as a weed-smothering groundcover under shrubs or along shaded path edges. Because the pink flower color is less common in the genus, it pairs well as an accent among blue- and violet-flowered ajuga plantings.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Azurea Flore Pleno Periwinkle (Double Sky-Blue Vinca Minor)

planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or divisions in part-shade soil amended with compost in spring; trailing stems root as they spread and knit into a mat over one to two seasons.

directions: This long-grown selection produces fully double, clear sky-blue flowers rather than the single blooms of the common species, giving each flower a fuller, more rounded look against the glossy dark evergreen leaves. Bloom is heaviest in mid-spring with scattered repeat flowers later in the season. Like other vinca minors it spreads by trailing stems that root at the nodes, making a dense mat useful for slopes and under shrubs. Because the doubled flowers are a bit smaller than single-flowered forms, planting in groups rather than as scattered single plants shows off the bloom display best.

common_name: Album Lamium (Plain White-Flowered Spotted Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Install in humus-rich, evenly moist shade soil in spring, the same conditions favored by the silver-leaf lamium cultivars.

directions: 'Album' keeps the species' typical green leaves with a central silvery stripe but produces pure white flowers instead of the usual pink or magenta, a simpler, cooler-toned option for a shaded planting. Bloom is concentrated in late spring with occasional sporadic flowers into summer. Growth habit matches other maculatum selections, forming a loose, trailing mat that roots as it spreads. It reads as a quieter companion to the brighter silver- or gold-leaf lamium cultivars rather than a standalone focal point.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Beedham's White Lamium (Chartreuse-Leaved White-Flowered Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant in part shade with some morning light in spring; a bit more sun than the silver-leaf lamiums helps keep the chartreuse color bright without scorching it.

directions: Small, toothed, oval leaves emerge a soft chartreuse-gold and hold that color through the season, offering a brighter foliage option than the silver- or green-leaved lamiums. White flowers open in loose whorls in late spring and continue sparingly into summer. The trailing stems root as they spread, forming a low, dense mat that works well as a bright color echo near gold-leaved shrubs or hostas. Occasional shearing after the main bloom flush keeps the mat tidy and encourages fresh new growth.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Elisabeth de Haas Lamium (Gold-Splashed Silver Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Install in humus-rich, evenly moist shade soil in spring; consistent moisture helps keep the variegated leaves from browning at the edges in summer heat.

directions: Foliage on this selection is silvery-green irregularly splashed with gold, a two-tone variegation pattern distinct from the more uniform silver- or solid-gold lamium cultivars. Rose-pink flowers appear in whorls in late spring above the mottled leaves. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems into a loose mat suited to the front of a shaded border or along a shaded path edge. Good air circulation and avoiding overhead watering help keep the patterned foliage free of leaf spot through a humid summer.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Sterling Silver Lamium (Solid Silver-Leaved Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Install in humus-rich, evenly moist shade soil in spring; give plants a bit more room than green-margined lamiums since the all-silver leaf reads brighter and shows wear more readily.

directions: Leaves on this selection are almost entirely silver with only a thin green edge, giving it a brighter, more uniform metallic look than lamiums with a broader green margin such as White Nancy. Soft pink flowers open in loose clusters in late spring with occasional repeat bloom. Growth is a trailing, mat-forming habit typical of the species, rooting at the nodes as it spreads. Siting it where some reflected light reaches the bed helps the pale foliage show up well in deeper shade.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide and plant clumps or plugs in part shade once soil has warmed in spring; this selection spreads by stolons like the species, so give it room to form a solid mat over a couple of seasons.

directions: This form keeps the same narrow, dark green, grass-like leaves as common mondo grass but produces white flower spikes in summer instead of the species' typical pale lilac blooms, followed by small blue-black berries. It spreads slowly by underground stolons into a dense, turf-like mat that tolerates foot traffic better than most flowering groundcovers once established. Evergreen in milder climates, it provides fine-textured, grassy structure along path edges or as a lawn substitute in small shaded areas. Established plantings are drought-tolerant but look best with regular moisture during active growth.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
